The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

For every $t\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy

$$\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_Kq(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\theta(t,x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(\partial_tq+\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)\bigr)\,dx,$$

where $D_tq=\partial_tq+u\cdot\nabla_xq$ and $\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$. The pointwise continuity equation $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, equivalently $\partial_t\rho+\nabla_x\!\cdot(\rho u)=0$, holds on $\Omega$ if and only if $M_K$ is constant on $I$ for every compact Jordan $K\subset U$, and if and only if $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho(0,\chi(0,a))J(0,a)$ for all $a\in U$ and $t\in I$. This is a mathematical equivalence; it adopts no physical mass-conservation postulate and asserts no weak-field or vacuum extension.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

By [F3], the boundary has content zero and its image integral agrees with the integral over $\chi_t(K)$. Thus [A1] makes $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$ constant on $I$.

The set $K$ is compact Jordan and $\rho$ is $C^1$, so [F2] gives
$$0=M_K'(t)=\int_{\chi_t(K)}R(t,x)\,dx,\qquad R:=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u).$$

Fix $(t,x_0)\in\mathcal O$ and write $x_0=\chi(t,a_0)$ with $a_0\in B$. If $R(t,x_0)>0$, continuity gives a neighborhood on which $R>R(t,x_0)/2$. Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. $$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Fix an admissible $V$ and let $K=\overline V$. By [F4], $K$ is compact Jordan and its open-region integrals equal the corresponding closure integrals. Apply [F3] componentwise to $f=\rho u$; the derivative of its material integral is
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)\bigr)\,dx.$$
Pointwise mass continuity and the product rule give
$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)=\rho D_tu.$$

Substitute the first balance in [A1] into step 1.1 and apply [F5] to $\sigma$. This yields
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\rho D_tu-\rho b-\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
The integrand is continuous because $b$ is continuous and the other fields are $C^1$. Every sufficiently small open ball $Q\Subset\Omega_t$ is such a material region: its inverse image under $\chi_t$ is a bounded $C^1$ region compactly contained in $B$. If a component of the continuous integrand were nonzero at a point, it would have a strict fixed sign on a smaller ball and its integral there could not vanish. Thus $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}_x\sigma$ pointwise.

For each component $i$,
$$\partial_t(\rho u_i)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(\rho u_i u_j)
=\rho(\partial_tu_i+u\cdot\nabla_xu_i)+u_i\bigl(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)\bigr).$$
The last term is zero by [F2]. Substituting step 1.2 and moving $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ to the flux gives the conservative momentum equation.

Apply [F3] to $\rho(x\times u)$ and use $D_tx=u$ and $u\times u=0$. The transport derivative is $\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho D_tu)\,dx$. Substitute step 1.2 and compare with the angular balance in [A1]; applying [F5] to the moment-stress flux gives
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)-x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
This residual is continuous, so the fixed-sign-ball argument of step 1.2 makes it zero pointwise. With $\epsilon_{ikl}$ the alternating symbol and $M_{ij}=\sum_{k,l}\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\sigma_{lj}$, direct differentiation gives
$$\bigl(\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)-x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)_i
=\sum_{j,l}\epsilon_{ijl}\sigma_{lj}.$$
For $i=1,2,3$ these equations are respectively $\sigma_{32}=\sigma_{23}$, $\sigma_{13}=\sigma_{31}$, and $\sigma_{21}=\sigma_{12}$, hence $\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T}$.

If $\sigma$ is symmetric, the component identity in step 1.4 gives $\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)=x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma$. The product rule and $u\times u=0$ give
$$\partial_t(\rho x\times u)+\operatorname{div}_x\bigl(\rho(x\times u)\otimes u\bigr)
=x\times\bigl(\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)\bigr).$$
Use step 1.3 and the stress-divergence identity, then integrate over $P_t$. The transport formula [F3] and divergence theorem [F5] recover the angular-momentum integral balance in [A1].

Dot $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$ from step 1.2 with $u$. The component product rule gives $u\cdot\operatorname{div}\sigma=\operatorname{div}(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)-\sigma:D_xu$. Since $\sigma$ is symmetric, its contraction with the skew part of $D_xu$ is zero, so $\sigma:D_xu=\sigma:D$. Also $D_tk=u\cdot D_tu$. Combining these identities with [F2] yields
$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho ku-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:D.$$

Apply [F3] to $\rho E$ in the total-energy balance [A1]. Rewrite $(\sigma n)\cdot u=(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)\cdot n$ and apply [F5] to $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$ and $q$. The integral of the continuous residual
$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho Eu-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)-\rho b\cdot u-\rho r$$
is zero on every $P_t$. The fixed-sign-ball argument from step 1.2 proves that this residual vanishes pointwise. Conversely, integrating this local equation and using [F3] and [F5] recovers the material total-energy balance.

Subtract the kinetic equation in step 1.6 from the total-energy equation in step 1.7 and use $E=e+k$. The body-work terms cancel and leave $\partial_t(\rho e)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho eu+q)=\sigma:D+\rho r$. Expanding the mass-transport term using [F2] gives $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}_xq+\rho r$. Conversely, adding this internal-energy equation to the kinetic equation in step 1.6 recovers the total-energy equation in step 1.7.

Adopt as a separate weak-branch model assumption that the displayed conservative variables, fluxes and sources below belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and satisfy the following identities for every indicated test function. Initial conservative data $\rho_0,m_0,\mathcal E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ represent initial mass, momentum, total-energy and entropy densities; the initial terms specify distributional data and do not assert a strong trace.

Mass balance, for every scalar $\phi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\cdot\nabla\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Momentum balance, for every vector $\psi$,
